title.en: Digestion of food: enzymes and their action

heading.en: Breaking big molecules into small ones

hook.en: A chapati is mostly starch, dal mostly protein, ghee mostly fat. None of them can cross the gut wall until *enzymes* cut them into small molecules.

title.en: Describe digestion in the mouth, stomach and small intestine
Name the enzymes, their substrates and products
Explain the role of pH and of enzyme activation

say.en: A chapati is mostly starch, dal mostly protein, ghee mostly fat. None of them can cross the gut wall until enzymes cut them into small molecules. In this lesson: Describe digestion in the mouth, stomach and small intestine.
Name the enzymes, their substrates and products.
Explain the role of pH and of enzyme activation.

body.en: Mouth: salivary amylase digests about 30% of starch to maltose (pH 6.8); lysozyme kills bacteria. Stomach: HCl (pH about 1.8) activates pepsinogen to pepsin, which turns proteins into proteoses and peptones; rennin curdles milk in infants; a little gastric lipase. Duodenum: bile emulsifies fats; pancreatic juice brings trypsinogen (activated by enterokinase to trypsin), chymotrypsinogen, carboxypeptidase, amylase, lipase and nucleases. The intestinal juice (succus entericus) finishes the job with dipeptidases, maltase, lactase, sucrase, lipases and nucleosidases. About 30% of starch is digested in the mouth and the rest in the small intestine.

points.en: Final products: glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, glycerol, nucleotides

title.en: Each enzyme has its own pH

narration.en: Move the pH from very acidic to alkaline. Pepsin works only in the strong acid of the stomach; amylase and trypsin need nearly neutral or alkaline conditions.

say.en: Move the pH from very acidic to alkaline. Pepsin works only in the strong acid of the stomach; amylase and trypsin need nearly neutral or alkaline conditions.
Carbohydrates: amylases, then maltase, sucrase, lactase.
Proteins: pepsin, trypsin and chymotrypsin, carboxypeptidase, dipeptidases.
Fats: bile emulsifies, lipases split them.
Nucleic acids: nucleases, nucleotidases and nucleosidases.

problem.en: Trace the digestion of a protein in milk from the mouth to absorption in an infant.

steps.en: Stomach: rennin curdles casein; pepsin (activated by HCl) gives proteoses and peptones.
Duodenum: trypsin, chymotrypsin and carboxypeptidase give dipeptides; intestinal dipeptidases give amino acids, which are absorbed.

answer.en: Rennin and pepsin → trypsin etc. → dipeptidases → amino acids

narration.en: Let us solve this together. Trace the digestion of a protein in milk from the mouth to absorption in an infant.

say.en: Let us solve this together. Trace the digestion of a protein in milk from the mouth to absorption in an infant.
Mouth: no protein digestion.
Stomach: rennin curdles casein; pepsin activated by HCl gives proteoses and peptones.
Duodenum: trypsin, chymotrypsin and carboxypeptidase give dipeptides; intestinal dipeptidases give amino acids, which are absorbed.
So the answer is Rennin and pepsin gives trypsin etc. gives dipeptidases gives amino acids.

body.en: Protein-digesting enzymes are made inactive (pepsinogen, trypsinogen) so they do not digest the cells that make them. HCl unlocks pepsin; enterokinase unlocks trypsin.

narration.en: Zymogens on safety. Protein-digesting enzymes are made inactive (pepsinogen, trypsinogen) so they do not digest the cells that make them. HCl unlocks pepsin; enterokinase unlocks trypsin.
